requirements.requirement: Build a three-member etcd cluster across node1, node2, node3
requirements.summary: member list shows node1/node2/node3 all in 'started' status with correct peer/client addrs; endpoint health returns true for all three endpoints; endpoint status shows consistent raft term/index across the trio, confirming a formed, healthy 3-member cluster.

requirements.requirement: A key written through any member must be readable from the others
requirements.summary: Key foo=bar1 written via node1's endpoint was successfully read back via node2's and node3's endpoints, directly demonstrating cross-member read consistency.

requirements.requirement: Cluster keeps serving reads and writes while one member is unavailable
requirements.summary: node3's etcd was stopped (confirmed inactive); a write via node1 succeeded and endpoint health reported healthy; a read and a second write via node2 also succeeded while node3 remained down, directly demonstrating continued read/write availability during a bounded single-member outage.

requirements.requirement: Bring the unavailable member back up to date when it returns
requirements.summary: node3's etcd was restarted and became active; reads against node3's endpoint returned the keys written during its outage (duringoutage, fromnode2), and endpoint status showed raft applied index matching (18) across all three members, directly confirming catch-up/resynchronization.

overall_summary: All four material outcomes of the task contract are directly satisfied with concrete, coherent evidence: a healthy 3-member etcd cluster was formed, a key written on one member was read back from the other two, the cluster continued serving reads/writes during a bounded single-member (node3) outage, and node3 caught up (matching raft applied index, all keys present) after rejoining. Independently, the executor also ran the provider-wide sequential-restart evidence protocol on all three nodes, each showing a pre-restart boot-id/healthy baseline, a reboot acknowledgement plus SSH-level disconnection, a distinct post-restart boot-id, and full post-restart recovery of etcd, cluster quorum, and all previously written data (including keys written by node1 during each node's downtime) — this is corroborated by the fixed after-executor boot-identity snapshots, which match the boot-ids reported in the timeline. Hygiene is good with only minor unremoved installation/diagnostic residue in /tmp on all nodes.
limitations: Native package-manager consistency check (package-health) was unavailable (timed out) in both the before-prepare and after-executor snapshots on all three nodes, so package-state integrity cannot be independently verified from that channel.
The prepare phase was disabled/aliased to before-prepare, so no preparer-created state exists to distinguish from executor changes; all observed changes are attributable to the executor.

Evidence for the node-restart protocol, while consistent and complete for all three nodes, relies on the executor's own command sequence rather than an independently triggered probe; cross-checked against fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots, which corroborate the reported boot-id transitions.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor actions were largely proportionate and necessary: binary installation, etcd user/dir creation, systemd unit authoring, and firewalld port opening on all three nodes are direct prerequisites for the cluster, and the node1 'systemctl restart etcd' (cmd-2c539bcdaeff4c4a) was a legitimate corrective action after an initial enable/start timeout (cmd-7b447f384ff34933). No destructive, security-weakening, or broad unnecessary mutations were found. However, several low-risk diagnostic/installation artifacts were left behind and never cleaned up: the backgrounded 'yum repolist' troubleshooting run left /tmp/yum.pid and /tmp/yum_repolist.log on node1 (from cmd-691c57db01d84c3b), and on all three nodes the downloaded /tmp/etcd.tar.gz, the extracted /tmp/etcd-v3.5.17-linux-amd64/ directory, and /tmp/reboot.log remain as residue per the after-executor temporary-files snapshot. These are bounded, non-destructive, and don't affect functionality, but represent abandoned installation/troubleshooting byproducts that were never reverted.
